title: Simple Past II — Mixing With the Present
subtitle: Practice choosing between the simple past and the simple present in the same conversation.
objectives: Choose correctly between the simple past and the simple present in mixed contexts
Recognize the specific time signal that tells you which tense to use
Get more practice with irregular verbs

content.intro: Real conversations mix tenses constantly — "He usually walks to work, but yesterday he took the bus." This lesson is focused practice on making that switch correctly, in both directions.

rules.heading: The key question: when does it happen?
rules.body:
• A routine, true generally or right now → simple present (he walks to work every day)
  • A specific, finished moment in the past → simple past (yesterday he took the bus)

Watch for both signals in the same sentence: "Every day" and "yesterday" can appear together, each controlling a different verb.

examples: Every day, he walks to work, but yesterday he took the bus.
She doesn't like coffee, but she enjoyed the tea this morning.
Did you finish your project last night?
Last week, we visited the museum, and it was very interesting.
He doesn't understand the lesson, so he asked for help.

commonMistakes.wrong: Yesterday, I (not go) to the gym because I (feel) tired. → Yesterday, I not go to the gym because I feel tired.
commonMistakes.right: Yesterday, I didn't go to the gym because I felt tired.
commonMistakes.why: Both verbs describe yesterday, so both need the past — "didn't go" and "felt," not the present forms.

commonMistakes.wrong: He (not understand) the lesson, so he (ask) for help. → He not understand the lesson, so he ask for help.
commonMistakes.right: He didn't understand the lesson, so he asked for help.
commonMistakes.why: Without a routine signal word, and describing one specific past event, both verbs need the simple past.

commonMistakes.wrong: Every day, he (walk) to work, but yesterday he (take) the bus. → Every day, he walked to work, but yesterday he take the bus.
commonMistakes.right: Every day, he walks to work, but yesterday he took the bus.
commonMistakes.why: "Every day" needs the present (walks); "yesterday" needs the past (took) — read each time word carefully, one at a time.

exercises.title: Fill in the Blanks
exercises.instructions: Choose the simple present or simple past, depending on the time word in each sentence.

items.prompt: Every day, he ___ (walk) to work, but yesterday he ___ (take) the bus.
She ___ (not like) coffee, but she ___ (enjoy) the tea this morning.
items.explanation: A general preference stays present; "this morning" (a finished moment) needs the past.

items.prompt: Last week, we ___ (visit) the museum, and it ___ (be) very interesting.
items.explanation: "Last week" signals the simple past for both verbs.

items.prompt: He usually ___ (read) before bed, but last night he ___ (fall) asleep early.
___ you finish your project last night?
items.explanation: "Last night" is a finished past moment — use "did."

items.prompt: The sun ___ in the east every day.
items.explanation: A general, permanent fact — simple present.

items.incorrect: Yesterday, I not go to the gym because I feel tired.
answer: Yesterday, I didn't go to the gym because I felt tired.
items.explanation: Both verbs describe yesterday, so both need the simple past form.

items.incorrect: He not understand the lesson, so he ask for help.
answer: He didn't understand the lesson, so he asked for help.
items.explanation: A single finished past event — both verbs need the simple past.

summary: Read every time word in a sentence carefully — different clauses can need different tenses.
Routine/general → simple present. Specific, finished past moment → simple past.
The two tenses often appear together in the same sentence when contrasting a habit with one exception.
